title: Korean prayer mountains
hookLine: Korean Christians rise before dawn for prayer meetings

cards: It's still dark outside, and the church lights are already on. In South Korea, some congregations meet for prayer before dawn on ordinary weekdays, before the subway fills and the offices open.
People come in work clothes. Some kneel, some sit. Then the whole room prays out loud at once, each person in their own words, a sound like rain on a roof.
Out on the hillsides there are places set apart only for prayer: prayer mountains, with small rooms and little caves where someone can pray through a night, or a week.

teach.b: In Korean, the early meeting is called saebyeok gido, dawn prayer. There's a verse that fits the habit. In Mark's Gospel, the whole town had crowded Jesus's door the night before.
Then, in the King James Bible: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Mark doesn't say what he prayed.
Only when and where: before day, and alone. A few lines later the disciples find him and say, "All men seek for thee." The prayer sits in the gap between last night's crowd and this morning's.

teach.h: IN THE MORNING, AND WILL LOOK UP.
teach.b: A psalm says it from the other side: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Some readers hear a watchman on a wall, waiting for the light.

Now put the two Korean habits beside Mark's verse. The prayer mountain gives his solitary place an address: people climb, sometimes fasting, pray in a small room cut into the hill, and come back down to their lives.
The dawn meeting gives his early hour company.

teach.h: ALONE ON A HILL, TOGETHER IN THE DARK.
teach.b: Alone on a hill, and together in the dark. Not every Korean church keeps the dawn hour, and Christians pray at other hours too.
But the habit has a simple logic: before the phone and the news and the list, the first words of the day can go somewhere else.

how: In South Korea, some Protestant churches hold prayer meetings before dawn on weekdays, where the congregation may pray aloud together, and prayer retreats on hillsides let people go away to pray for a night or longer.

games.q: you're one of the disciples. last night the whole town crowded the door. this morning Jesus is gone. where is he?
o: he's left for another town without a word.
he rose before day and went to pray alone.
he's still asleep inside the house.
games.why: "rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." when they find him, they say, all men seek for thee.

practice: Whatever the hour where you are, go back to the first minute of today: what got there first, a worry, a screen, someone else's voice?
Don't scold yourself; just notice, and give the next two minutes the job the morning might have had.
If you pray, borrow the psalm, in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee; if not, face a window, look up, and wait the way a watchman waits for light.

wordCard.voice: Saebyeok gido. Korean for dawn prayer, prayer that gets there before the day does, kept on hillsides and in city churches before sunrise.

orig.note: Greek: early, in the morning — the word Mark uses for the hour Jesus rose to pray.

carryVoice: Your line: dawn prayer. The hour before the sun belongs to no one else yet. See you tomorrow.
